How migrating birds plan their flights across oceans

Published 2026-10-05 23:30 UTC

Every autumn, millions of small songbirds fly nonstop across oceans to reach their wintering grounds, a journey that can last several days without food, water or rest. New tracking data reveals that the birds plan these flights with remarkable precision, waiting for the right winds before they leave.

Researchers fitted lightweight tags weighing less than a gram to hundreds of birds at coastal stopover sites. The tags recorded location, altitude and air pressure. When the scientists compared departure dates with weather records, they found that birds overwhelmingly left on nights with favorable tailwinds, even if that meant waiting a week or more.

The birds appear to sense approaching weather systems. Changes in air pressure and wind direction often preceded departures by a day. Birds that left in poor conditions were more likely to turn back or to stop at islands along the way, suggesting that leaving at the right time is critical for survival.

In flight, the birds adjusted their altitude to find the best winds, sometimes climbing above 5,000 meters. Some species flew at night and rose higher during the day to avoid overheating. Their routes curved with the wind rather than following the shortest path, saving energy over the full journey.

The findings raise concerns about climate change. Shifts in weather patterns could reduce the number of nights with favorable winds or change their timing, forcing birds to depart in worse conditions or to spend longer fattening up at stopover sites that may themselves be threatened.

Ornithologists say the data also highlights how much young birds must get right on their first migration, when they travel without experienced adults. How they learn to read the weather remains an open question.

Some species even appear to correct for crosswinds over open water, adjusting their heading so that they arrive at the intended coastline rather than drifting hundreds of kilometers off course.
